messages.content: In experiments with self-adapting language models, what improvement in performance was observed when using the SEAL method for few-shot learning compared to standard in-context learning? For example, how did their success rates differ on a benchmark task?

preferred_output.content: Research results showed a very large improvement in performance when using the SEAL self-adaptation method versus relying on in-context examples alone. For instance, on an abstract reasoning benchmark (a few-shot task from the ARC dataset), a language model using SEAL achieved roughly a 72% success rate, whereas the same model using only in-context learning (just seeing the examples in the prompt without adapting) achieved essentially 0% success on those tasks. Even a baseline where the model was allowed to do a test-time fine-tuning without the guided “self-edit” strategy only reached about 20%. This stark contrast – roughly 72% with self-adaptation vs near 0% with prompt-only – demonstrates how much more effective it is for the model to learn from the examples via self-training. It highlights that SEAL’s few-shot adaptation approach can translate a handful of examples into significant performance gains, whereas just providing those examples in the prompt yielded almost no progress on that challenging task.

non_preferred_output.content: The SEAL method demonstrated a significant improvement in few-shot learning performance over standard in-context learning. In the experiments described in the SEAL paper, the self-adapting model achieved much higher success rates on a benchmark task than a model using only in-context learning. For instance, on a challenging few-shot task (such as a synthetic reasoning or QA task), the SEAL model might reach a success rate of around 80% or more, whereas the same model relying solely on in-context learning (just using the examples in the prompt without any self-adaptation) might only achieve a success rate of about 30%. This means the self-adapting model solved more than twice as many test questions correctly compared to the non-adapting baseline. The key takeaway is that by generating and learning from its own examples, the SEAL model was able to generalize from the few provided examples much more effectively, leading to a dramatic boost in accuracy on new test cases.
